sections.html:
Albany sits in the Willamette Valley where the Calapooia River meets the Willamette, east of Corvallis and south of Salem. It is the seat of Linn County, but a smaller slice of the city north of downtown lies in Benton County. The city has 56,472 residents as of the 2020 census, with an estimate of 57,777 for 2024, and 41.3 percent of occupied homes are rented.

The county line decides who handles your paperwork. A house in North Albany is billed and assessed by Benton County, while most other Albany homes go through Linn County. Look at your tax statement to see which county it names before you phone about values or due dates.

  • Linn County: most of Albany, with a 2020 population of 128,610.
  • Benton County: the northern part of the city, county seat Corvallis.
  • City services: Albany runs its own police, fire, library, water supply and wastewater treatment.

sections.h2: Linn County tax dates for Albany homes
sections.html:
Linn County bills Albany property tax once a year. Its 2024 notice reported statements mailed October 18, based on a January 1 assessment date.

Payment choiceDue dates
Full payment, 3% discountNovember 15
Two thirds, 2% discountNovember 15, remainder May 15
One third, no discountNovember 15, February 18, May 15

Interest applies to any late installment, and the county mails no reminders for the February or May payments. The Linn County Assessment and Taxation Office is at 541-967-3808.

sections.h2: North Albany and the appeal deadline
sections.html:
Benton County, which covers North Albany, runs a similar calendar, with installments November 15, February 15 and May 15. Value appeals to the Board of Property Tax Appeals close December 31, and Measure 50 holds assessed value growth to 3 percent annually.

The title company divides the year's bill between you and the buyer based on how long each of you owned the house. Your escrow officer can show the exact proration.

Winters are mild and wet and summers warm and dry, which means most repair bills come from moisture. Precipitation runs about 39.9 inches a year over roughly 147 days, and December is the wettest month at 6.8 inches. Snow is light, about 5.5 inches a year. The record high of 110 degrees, set on June 27, 2021, is a reminder that attic ventilation and cooling matter too.

  • Roofs and gutters take the brunt of the wet season.
  • Crawl spaces under pre-war houses often hold moisture.
  • Low ground near the rivers deserves a flood-map check before you price or list.
  • Houses from the 1840 to 1920 era in the historic districts can carry old systems that a buyer's inspector will flag.

A cash sale does not require fixing any of it. A retail buyer's inspector, though, tends to raise exactly these items.

If your house is in one of Albany's National Register districts, exterior changes need city review, which can slow a renovation plan. Most of the historic architecture sits in three districts: Monteith, Hackleman and Downtown Commercial. Part of the Albany Municipal Airport is also a historic district. The four historic districts hold more than 700 historic buildings, most of them built between 1840 and 1920.

Since 1985, designated buildings in the districts and those on the landmark inventory have gone through review for exterior alterations, additions and demolition. Planning staff or the Landmarks Commission handles it. The city favors repair over replacement and asks for matching materials when replacement cannot be avoided. Program rules are on the City of Albany historic preservation page.

The review applies to whoever owns the house next. A worn porch or failing siding in Monteith or Hackleman can mean a repair list that the buyer must carry out under those rules, and selling as-is moves that job to the buyer.

A sale is a narrow reason to end a month-to-month tenancy in Oregon. ORS 90.427 requires two things: an accepted offer from a buyer who will make the home a primary residence, and written notice delivered at least 90 days before the tenancy ends.

  • Notice has to be given within 120 days of the accepted offer.
  • Delivering notice also means paying the tenant one month's rent, except for landlords with four or fewer covered units.
  • In the tenant's first year, 30 days' notice can end a month-to-month tenancy without cause.
  • Break the rules and the landlord may owe three months' rent plus damages.

An investor buyer usually takes the house with the tenant in place, which can make a cash sale simpler for an Albany landlord than a listing aimed at owner-occupants.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Albany
sections.html:
Title and escrow work the same way in a cash sale, minus the loan and the appraisal. An offer arrives, you settle on a closing date, the title company clears the deed, and the sale gets recorded.

The shorter path fits an inherited house, a rental with tenant problems or a home with put-off maintenance, the usual reasons owners skip a regular listing.

sections.h2: What to line up before you sell
sections.html: Start with the county. Confirm from your tax statement whether Linn or Benton County bills the house, then note the next installment date so you can settle who pays it in the contract. If the house is in Monteith or Hackleman, look at the exterior condition and decide whether to leave that work to the buyer. If tenants live there, read ORS 90.427 or ask your title company about notice rules before you tell anyone about a sale. Last, ask your escrow officer how the proration will appear on the settlement statement, so closing day brings no surprises.

sections.h2: Albany's history and economy in brief
sections.html: Albany was settled in the 1840s, named a county seat in 1851 and incorporated in 1864. The railroad arrived in 1871. The economy rests on retail, health care and manufacturing, with a strong rare metals sector, so jobs are spread across factories, a hospital and a community college and house demand does not hang on one company.

Interstate 5 and Oregon 99E run north and south through Albany, and US 20 runs east to west, crossing the Willamette into Corvallis on the Ellsworth Street and Lyon Street bridges. Amtrak stops at the station on 10th Avenue SW, and local buses link to Corvallis. Eugene and Portland have the nearest commercial airports.

faqs.q: Linn or Benton: which county handles my Albany sale?
faqs.a: Most Albany houses are in Linn County, but homes in North Albany are in Benton County. Your tax statement names the county, so read it before asking about assessment or due dates.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due on an Albany house?
faqs.a: November 15 is the main due date in both counties. Linn County allows a 3 percent discount for full payment by then, and thirds can be paid in November, February and May.

faqs.q: Do I need to fix an older Albany house before selling?
faqs.a: No repair is required to sell, but a house in the Monteith or Hackleman districts has exterior work that falls under city historic review for its next owner. Selling as-is leaves that work to the buyer.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Albany rental with a tenant living in it?
faqs.a: Yes. Because ORS 90.427 restricts ending a tenancy for a sale, many owners sell with the tenant staying. Ninety days' notice applies only when the buyer will move in.

faqs.q: What if I have back property tax on an Albany house?
faqs.a: Get the balance from the county and pass it to the title company, which pays it out of your proceeds at closing. In Linn County the office to call is Assessment and Taxation, 541-967-3808.
